title: Cap. IX Arg. 13 Sol: sloth cannot un-predestinate the elect, yet can harm them many ways — effects/benefits of predestination are to be advanced by ministers' diligence (Thomas)
pass_a_gloss: Finally, although no one is so impious, or so unskilled in the Theological matter, as to think that by the sloth of ministers any of the predestined can become non-predestined, or can fall from the glory prepared for the predestined, yet no one is so imprudent as not to understand that the sloth of ministers can in various ways harm any predestined person. For although the everlasting decree itself of God predestinating is neither procured, nor helped, nor hindered by any human acts, yet the effects of predestination, or the benefits prepared for men in predestination, can and ought to be promoted by the diligence of ministers. Whence Thomas, Part. 1. quaest. 23. artic. 8. Predestination does not take away second causes, but so provides for the effect that even the order of second causes is subject unto providence. Ministers therefore ought to know that their diligence is subordinated by God unto promoting the salvation of the elect.
pass_b_english: Finally: no one is so impious, or so unskilled in theology, as to think ministers' sloth can make any of the predestined non-predestined, or make them fall from the glory prepared for them. Yet no one is so foolish as not to see that ministers' sloth can harm any predestined person in many ways. For though the eternal decree of God predestinating is neither procured, helped, nor hindered by any human acts, the effects of predestination — or the benefits prepared for men in it — can and ought to be advanced by ministers' diligence. So Thomas (Part. 1 q.23 a.8): Predestination does not take away second causes, but so provides for the effect that even the order of second causes lies under providence. Ministers therefore ought to know their diligence is subordinated by God to promoting the elect's salvation.
source_text: Denique, quamvis nemo tam impius, aut rei Theologicae imperitus sit, qui cogitet ministrorum socordia quemlibet ex praedestinatis fieri posse non praedestinatum, aut excidere posse gloria praedestinatis praeparata, tamen nemo tam imprudens est, qui non intelligat ministrorum socordiam posse variis modis cuivis praedestinato obesse. Nam licet ipsum aeternum decretum Dei praedestinantis neque procuretur, neque juvetur, neque impediatur ullis actibus humanis, tamen effecta praedestinationis, vel beneficia in praedestinatione hominibus praeparata, possunt et debent ministrorum diligentia promoveri. Unde Thomas, Part. 1. quaest. 23. artic. 8. Praedestinatio non tollit causas secundas, sed sic providet effectui ut etiam ordo causarum secundarum subjaceat providentiae. Ministri igitur scire debent suam diligentiam esse a Deo subordinatam saluti electorum promovendae.
